summary: Describes the Russian federal standard algorithms for encryption, decryption and message authentication codes, GOST 28147-89. It was written as information for developers and users of Russian cryptography in Internet applications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5830 describes GOST 28147-89, a Russian standard for encrypting and decrypting data and generating message authentication codes. It records the algorithm for information purposes and is not an Internet standard.

questions: how many rounds does gost 28147-89 use
subtitle: The GOST block cipher's encryption modes and message authentication code procedure.

tldr.problem: Developers and users needed an informational description of the Russian GOST 28147-89 encryption, decryption and message-authentication algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: The standard describes a 64-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key, 32 encryption rounds and four modes: ECB, counter, cipher feedback and MAC generation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5830 is an Informational source document, not an Internet Standards Track specification, and the supplied metadata says RFC 8891 updates it.

today: RFC 5830 is an Informational document published in March 2010 and has been updated by RFC 8891. It is published for information, not as an Internet Standards Track specification.

sections.title: Purpose and Applicability
sections.content:
GOST 28147-89 defines rules for encryption, decryption and generation of a message authentication code (MAC). The RFC presents the standard as information for developers and users working with cryptography in Internet applications.

The document says the algorithm is intended for systems that exchange information over insecure public telecommunications channels. It also states that the standard is obligatory in the Russian Federation for data-processing systems providing public services.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes a cipher for encrypting and decrypting messages, plus a method for making a MAC. A receiver can use the MAC to check whether protected data was altered.

sections.title: The Cipher's Building Blocks
sections.content:
The cryptographic model uses a 256-bit key held in eight 32-bit registers and working registers for data. It also uses arithmetic operations, a substitution box (S-box) and a cyclic shift of 11 steps.

The standard does not define the S-box tables. The RFC notes that some S-box sets are described in RFC 4357 and treats the key and S-box values as secret elements supplied through an established procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher stores its 256-bit key in eight registers and transforms data with arithmetic, substitution and rotation steps. The standard does not specify the S-box tables.

sections.title: Electronic Codebook Mode
sections.content:
In electronic codebook (ECB) mode, plaintext is divided into 64-bit blocks. Each block passes through 32 rounds that combine a key register, the S-box, an 11-step cyclic shift and the other 32-bit half of the block.

Encryption uses the key registers in a defined order: the sequence X0 through X7 is used three times, followed by X7 through X0. Decryption uses the same core operation with a different key-register order.
sections.plainLanguage: The block mode encrypts one 64-bit block at a time. Each block goes through 32 rounds, and decryption uses the key registers in a different order.

sections.title: Counter, Feedback and MAC Modes
sections.content:
Counter mode encrypts a 64-bit initialization vector and uses the result to generate blocks of a running key. The plaintext is combined with that running key, and the initialization vector and ciphertext are transmitted.

In cipher feedback mode, each ciphertext block feeds into the generation of the next running-key block. MAC generation processes message blocks using the first 16 rounds of the ECB algorithm and attaches a selected-length MAC to the encrypted data; the receiver recomputes and compares it.
sections.plainLanguage: Counter and cipher feedback modes generate a running key and combine it with message data. MAC mode produces a value that the receiver recalculates to check the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section states only that the entire document concerns security considerations. It provides no separate evaluation of the cipher's strength.

The text says the key and S-box tables are secret elements, while also noting that the standard itself leaves S-box values undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives no separate analysis of the cipher's security. It says the key and S-box values are secret and that the standard does not define the S-box tables.
